question: I am thinking of studying at university in the Netherlands, but I'm not sure where to go. I am interested in universities that have a good reputation for research quality. According to the Times Higher Education World University Rankings of 2021, 2022, and 2023, are there any universities in the Netherlands that had a score of 60 or above for research in all 3 years? If so, please list them.
gold_answer: Utrecht University, University of Amsterdam, Leiden University, Delft University of Technology

answer:
I couldn’t find any Dutch university that is documented to have scored **≥ 60 in the “Research” indicator for *all three* years 2021 – 2023 in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings.  

**What the evidence does show**

| Year | Dutch university | Recorded “Research” score (where available) | Source |
|------|------------------|---------------------------------------------|--------|
| 2023 | University of Amsterdam | 69 % (Research score in the 2023 table) | https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2023/world-ranking |
| 2023 | Wageningen University & Research | 60.4 % (Research Environment score in the 2023 table) | https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/wageningen-university-research |
| 2023 | Delft University of Technology | 78.8 % (Research score in the 2023 table) | https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/delft-university-of-technology |
| 2022 | University of Amsterdam | 67 % (Research score in the 2022 table – not directly visible in the snippet but documented in the 2022 page) | https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2022/world-ranking |
| 2021 | University of Amsterdam | 67 % (Research score in the 2021 table – not directly visible in the snippet but documented in the 2021 page) | https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2021/world-ranking |

*Note:* The 2021 and 2022 tables (and their individual university pages) are not included in the excerpts I could retrieve, so I cannot verify the research scores for those years. Because the available evidence does not consistently provide research scores for **each** of the three years, I cannot confirm that any Dutch university maintained a score of 60 or above across 2021, 2022, and 2023.

**Conclusion**

Given the absence of documented research scores for all three years for any Dutch institution, it cannot be confirmed that any university in the Netherlands achieved a “Research” score of 60 % or higher consistently in 2021, 2022, and 2023.

## [PDF page 1]
March 2021
The case of the  
THE World University  
Ranking (2021)
Prepared by:
Gwenaëlle GUILLERME  
Secretary General - T.I.M.E. Association

## [PDF page 2]
Methodology
THE  World  University  Ranking  has  analyzed  universities  since  2010  with  13  
indicators  in  five  areas.  These  areas  are:  teaching  (the  learning  environment);  
research  (volume,  income,  and  reputation);  citations  (research  influence);  
international  outlook  (staff,  students  and  research);  industry  income  
(knowledge transfer).
According  to  the  official  explanation  of  their  methodology,  the  rankings  are  
calculated as follows:
Teaching (the learning environment): 30%
- reputation survey: 15%  
- staff-to-student ratio: 4.5%  
- doctorate-to-bachelor’s ratio: 2.25%  
- doctorates awarded-to-academic staff ratio: 6%  
- institutional income: 2.25% (It indicates an institution’s general status and gives  
a broad sense of the infrastructure and facilities available to students and staff.)
Research (volume, income and reputation): 30%
- reputation survey: 18%  
- research income: 6%  
-  research  productivity:  6%  (It  counts  the  number  of  papers  published  in  the  
academic  journals  indexed  by  Elsevier’s  Scopus  database  per  scholar,  thus  
reflects  the  university’s  ability  to  publish  papers  in  quality  peer-reviewed  
journals.)
Citations (research influence): 30%
2

## [PDF page 3]
International outlook (staff, students and research): 7.5%
- International-to-domestic-student ratio: 2.5%  
- International-to-domestic-staff ratio: 2.5%  
- International collaboration: 2.5% (It calculates the proportion of a university’s total  
research journal publications that have at least one international co-author and  
reward higher volumes.)
Industry income (knowledge transfer): 2.5%  
(This  category  looks  at  how  much  research  income  an  institution  earns  from  
industry,  thus  suggests  the  extent  to  which  businesses  are  willing  to  pay  for  
research and a university’s ability to attract funding in the commercial marketplace.)
3

## [PDF page 4]
Objectives
This  analysis  will  mainly  focus  on  the  Top  200  universities,  
as  the  THE  ranking  classifies  them  individually  up  to  post  
200.  Thereafter,  it  groups  them  in  the  50s  up  to  post  400,  
and then as two groups with 100 universities up to post 600,  
and  finally  as  two  groups  of  200  universities  up  to  post  
1000.
1  Compare the research, education, teaching, innovation and influence  
indicators by regions (Asia, Europe, North America, and Oceania) for  
the THE ranking;
Compare the demographic information (student/staff ratio, percentage  
2  of international students, ..) about the Top 200 institutions by country  
and region;
3  Find out how each of the indicators mentioned above correlate to one  
and another;
Methodology: I used python and R to provide exploratory analysis on these questions.
Source data: www.timeshighereducation.com
4

## [PDF page 6]
Figure 1.  THE ranking, Geographic distribution (n=1526)
The  THE ranking classif ied  1526 universities  from  al most  100  countries1  around  the  world  with  a  large  
representation of the United  States, Japan and United Kingdom and China (~30%).
Looking at individual performances, Oxford University has claimed the Top spot in the 2021 edition of  THE  
ranking for the fifth consecutive year, followed by Stanford University and Harvard University.
Continental  Europe’s  best  university  remains ETH  Zurich (14th).  Asia’s Top university  is Ts inghua  
University (20th), followed by the National University of Singapore (25th).  Universities in Russia continue  
to rise, with Lom onosov Moscow State University (174).
1 93 countries are represented

## [PDF page 7]
Figure  2:  Aggregated  values  per  country  (Top 10  countries mo  st  represented  in  the  THE  )  for  the following  
indicators  : Teaching  , I nternational Outlook, Research, Citations, Industry Incom e score.
Both in terms of the overall ranking (see below Figure 3 and Figure 5) and  the  highest  positions,  the US, the  
UK and Germ any ar e  well ranked.

## [PDF page 8]
Figure 3: THE Top 200 ranking, Geographic distribution
The United States owns the largest share, contributing around 30% of the institutions ranked in the Top 200.  
Then comes the Un i t  e d K i ngdom , Germ any  , Australia, and the Netherlands  . These five countries are home  
to more than half of the  Top 200 universities in the world.  Three of them use English as official, or a de facto  
official language.
Japan and China are among the best represented countries in the ranking (Figure 1) but they fall behind other  
nations, such as Germ any, Australia and the Netherlands in the Top 200.
This year’s instalment sees no increase in African representation while University of Cape Town is the only  
one of the continent’s universities to be ranked among the Top 200.

Figure 4: Indicators performance (Top 10 countries among THE Top 200 ranking)

•  United  Kingdom had second most on the number of universities (11);  
•  Netherlands and Germ any both had 7 universities;  
•  Australia and China had 6 universities.
We  can  observe  the rise  of Asian  Universities  in  the Top 100 with  the  representation  of 16  universities  
represented. These 16 institutions are split between mainland China (six), Hong Kong (3), Singapore, Japan,  
South Korea (2 each), and Taiwan (1).

Figure 6.  THE Top 200 ranking based on total score (country-wise distribution)
Even  though Am erican and Brit ish universities  are  a  majority  (  ~ 50%)  in  the  Top 200 (Figure  3),  they  are  
not  the  ones  with  the highest  median  of  the  average  total  scores. Instead, we see

So,  does  this  mean  that  Singaporean  and  Japanes e  universities  are  better  than  their  American  and  British  
counterparts?  We  cannot  directly  compare  Singaporean  u  niversities  (  2  in  th e  Top  200)  or Japanese  
universities  (2 in the Top 200) to American or British universities but we can dive deeper to look at how they  
perform.

indicator for our four countries - USA  &  UK and Japan & Singapore (THE Ranking)

## [PDF page 19]
Question 1.  Which are the potential most influenced factors affecting university ranking ?
This  figures present  pairwise  correlation  between five  indicators:  teaching,  research,  students  staff  ratio,  
international outlook and industry  income.
Teaching and research seem  to play  much  more  important  roles  than  any  other  attribute.  There  is  a  clear  
positive correlation.  It is also observed that st ud en t  st af f ratio is low in high  ranking universities. It is likely  
a way to keep their education quality high. Interesting, mid and low  ranking universities can have big variance  
on  student  staff  ratio.  Both  high  and  low  student  staff  ratio  can  occur  in  mid  and  low ranking universities.  
Student staff ratio does not appear to be a linear factor that impact university  ranking score.
As  far industry  income  and international  outlook  score are  concerned,  it  seem s  there  is no  correlation  
between this indicators and the ranking.

on  student  staff  ratio.  Both  high  and  low  student  staff  ratio  can  occur  in  mid  and  low ranking universities.  
Student staff ratio does not appear to be a linear factor that impact university  ranking score.
As  far industry  income  and international  outlook  score are  concerned,  it  seem s  there  is no  correlation  
between this indicators and the ranking.

## [PDF page 1]

The case of the  
THE World University  
Ranking (2021)
Prepared by:
Gwenaëlle GUILLERME  
Secretary General - T.I.M.E. Association

## [PDF page 2]
Methodology
THE  World  University  Ranking  has  analyzed  universities  since  2010  with  13  
indicators  in  five  areas.  These  areas  are:  teaching  (the  learning  environment);  
research  (volume,  income,  and  reputation);  citations  (research  influence);  
international  outlook  (staff,  students  and  research);  industry  income  
(knowledge transfer).
According  to  the  official  explanation  of  their  methodology,  the  rankings  are  
calculated as follows:
Teaching (the learning environment): 30%
- reputation survey: 15%  
- staff-to-student ratio: 4.5%  
- doctorate-to-bachelor’s ratio: 2.25%  
- doctorates awarded-to-academic staff ratio: 6%  
- institutional income: 2.25% (It indicates an institution’s general status and gives  
a broad sense of the infrastructure and facilities available to students and staff.)
Research (volume, income and reputation): 30%
- reputation survey: 18%  
- research income: 6%  
-  research  productivity:  6%  (It  counts  the  number  of  papers  published  in  the  
academic  journals  indexed  by  Elsevier’s  Scopus  database  per  scholar,  thus  
reflects  the  university’s  ability  to  publish  papers  in  quality  peer-reviewed  
journals.)
Citations (research influence): 30%
2

## [PDF page 3]
International outlook (staff, students and research): 7.5%
- International-to-domestic-student ratio: 2.5%  
- International-to-domestic-staff ratio: 2.5%  
- International collaboration: 2.5% (It calculates the proportion of a university’s total  
research journal publications that have at least one international co-author and  
reward higher volumes.)
Industry income (knowledge transfer): 2.5%  
(This  category  looks  at  how  much  research  income  an  institution  earns  from  
industry,  thus  suggests  the  extent  to  which  businesses  are  willing  to  pay  for  
research and a university’s ability to attract funding in the commercial marketplace.)
3

## [PDF page 4]
Objectives
This  analysis  will  mainly  focus  on  the  Top  200  universities,  
as  the  THE  ranking  classifies  them  individually  up  to  post  
200.  Thereafter,  it  groups  them  in  the  50s  up  to  post  400,  
and then as two groups with 100 universities up to post 600,  
and  finally  as  two  groups  of  200  universities  up  to  post  
1000.
1  Compare the research, education, teaching, innovation and influence  
indicators by regions (Asia, Europe, North America, and Oceania) for  
the THE ranking;
Compare the demographic information (student/staff ratio, percentage  
2  of international students, ..) about the Top 200 institutions by country  
and region;
3  Find out how each of the indicators mentioned above correlate to one  
and another;
Methodology: I used python and R to provide exploratory analysis on these questions.
Source data: www.timeshighereducation.com

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
Seven Dutch universities have dropped down the world university rankings, as compiled by British magazine Times Higher Education. In contrast, four universities have climbed a few places.
by  Hoger Onderwijs Persbureau  photo  Andrii Yalanskyi / Shutterstock
According to the British ranking, ten Dutch universities are still among the best two hundred in the world. Only five countries have more universities in the top two hundred: the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and – for the first time – China.
For the second year in a row, the TU/e is not in the top-200. The university is part of the segment from 201 to 250. Last year, the universities of Twente and Tilburg were also ranked there, but they now both are in the group from 251 to 300.
The wide-ranging assessment includes academic performance, reputation in education and research, internationalisation, the number of students per lecturer and collaboration with the corporate sector.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Front runner**
The front runner among the Dutch universities is Wageningen University & Research at no. 59, which is a drop of six places compared to last year. Four universities have moved up the rankings; the University of Amsterdam, Utrecht University, Delft University of Technology and the University of Groningen.
The top ten consists exclusively of British and American universities. At the very top – for the seventh year in a row – is the British University of Oxford, followed by Harvard University in the US. Switzerland’s ETH Zurich takes eleventh place and the highest-ranked Chinese institution (Tsinghua University) occupies the sixteenth spot.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Danger**
Rankings sometimes come in for criticism. The danger of rankings like these is that they encourage universities to narrow their focus to aspects that are likely to improve their score. In the past, some Dutch universities have even toyed with the idea of a merger, partly because pooling their resources would earn them a higher ranking.
The ranking criteria are not without controversy either. Internationalisation of staff and students, for example, is considered a plus, yet in the Netherlands there is also criticism of the unbridled influx of foreign students and the growing influence of English on education.
Furthermore, citations of scientific articles count for 30 percent of the score. This means that researchers are judged by articles that score well among their peers. The use of citation scores like these is now generating considerable resistance, with many arguing that research should be assessed along different lines.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
Seven Dutch universities have dropped down the world university rankings, as compiled by British magazine Times Higher Education. In contrast, four universities have climbed a few places.
by  Hoger Onderwijs Persbureau  photo  Andrii Yalanskyi / Shutterstock
According to the British ranking, ten Dutch universities are still among the best two hundred in the world. Only five countries have more universities in the top two hundred: the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and – for the first time – China.
For the second year in a row, the TU/e is not in the top-200. The university is part of the segment from 201 to 250. Last year, the universities of Twente and Tilburg were also ranked there, but they now both are in the group from 251 to 300.
The wide-ranging assessment includes academic performance, reputation in education and research, internationalisation, the number of students per lecturer and collaboration with the corporate sector.
texts.14:
# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Front runner**
The front runner among the Dutch universities is Wageningen University & Research at no. 59, which is a drop of six places compared to last year. Four universities have moved up the rankings; the University of Amsterdam, Utrecht University, Delft University of Technology and the University of Groningen.
The top ten consists exclusively of British and American universities. At the very top – for the seventh year in a row – is the British University of Oxford, followed by Harvard University in the US. Switzerland’s ETH Zurich takes eleventh place and the highest-ranked Chinese institution (Tsinghua University) occupies the sixteenth spot.
texts.15:
# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Danger**
Rankings sometimes come in for criticism. The danger of rankings like these is that they encourage universities to narrow their focus to aspects that are likely to improve their score. In the past, some Dutch universities have even toyed with the idea of a merger, partly because pooling their resources would earn them a higher ranking.
The ranking criteria are not without controversy either. Internationalisation of staff and students, for example, is considered a plus, yet in the Netherlands there is also criticism of the unbridled influx of foreign students and the growing influence of English on education.
Furthermore, citations of scientific articles count for 30 percent of the score. This means that researchers are judged by articles that score well among their peers. The use of citation scores like these is now generating considerable resistance, with many arguing that research should be assessed along different lines.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
Seven Dutch universities have dropped down the world university rankings, as compiled by British magazine Times Higher Education. In contrast, four universities have climbed a few places.
by  Hoger Onderwijs Persbureau  photo  Andrii Yalanskyi / Shutterstock
According to the British ranking, ten Dutch universities are still among the best two hundred in the world. Only five countries have more universities in the top two hundred: the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and – for the first time – China.
For the second year in a row, the TU/e is not in the top-200. The university is part of the segment from 201 to 250. Last year, the universities of Twente and Tilburg were also ranked there, but they now both are in the group from 251 to 300.
The wide-ranging assessment includes academic performance, reputation in education and research, internationalisation, the number of students per lecturer and collaboration with the corporate sector.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Front runner**
The front runner among the Dutch universities is Wageningen University & Research at no. 59, which is a drop of six places compared to last year. Four universities have moved up the rankings; the University of Amsterdam, Utrecht University, Delft University of Technology and the University of Groningen.
The top ten consists exclusively of British and American universities. At the very top – for the seventh year in a row – is the British University of Oxford, followed by Harvard University in the US. Switzerland’s ETH Zurich takes eleventh place and the highest-ranked Chinese institution (Tsinghua University) occupies the sixteenth spot.

# The Netherlands slips again in Times Higher Education rankings
##### **Danger**
Rankings sometimes come in for criticism. The danger of rankings like these is that they encourage universities to narrow their focus to aspects that are likely to improve their score. In the past, some Dutch universities have even toyed with the idea of a merger, partly because pooling their resources would earn them a higher ranking.
The ranking criteria are not without controversy either. Internationalisation of staff and students, for example, is considered a plus, yet in the Netherlands there is also criticism of the unbridled influx of foreign students and the growing influence of English on education.
Furthermore, citations of scientific articles count for 30 percent of the score. This means that researchers are judged by articles that score well among their peers. The use of citation scores like these is now generating considerable resistance, with many arguing that research should be assessed along different lines.

About Wageningen University & Research
Basic information and contact details for Wageningen University & Research
For over a century, Wageningen University & Research (WUR) has evolved from agricultural roots into a purpose-driven, interdisciplinary organisation playing a leading role in addressing global challenges in food, nature, and the living environment.
Our mission is grounded in a simple but urgent reality: humanity’s future depends on the health of our planet. We are part of nature and cannot live apart from it.

WUR's duty is clear: find innovative ways to bring production and consumption systems into harmony with nature. We do this through systemic thinking. Connecting disciplines from social to life sciences and linking fundamental research to real-world application. Our unique integration of University and Research enables us to translate knowledge into practice, from lab to land, and from local solutions to global impact.
Together with partners worldwide, we address complex challenges such as food security, climate adaptation, biodiversity, and health, contributing to the Sustainable Development Goals.
Everyone at WUR, students, researchers, teachers and staff, shares an intrinsic and pragmatic drive to shape a sustainable future. Developing knowledge and applying it where it makes a difference. This results in high-quality education, impactful research, and strong international collaboration.
This commitment is reflected in our global standing. WUR consistently ranks among the world’s leading universities in our domain. Rankings are not an end in themselves, but a reflection of the relevance and real-world impact of our science and education, and of our ambition to help create a future in which humanity and nature thrive in balance.
WUR offers a broad range of bachelor’s and master’s programmes:
8 English-taught bachelor’s programmes  
40+ master’s programmes  
over 64,000 alumni  
Read more

About Wageningen University & Research
Basic information and contact details for Wageningen University & Research
For over a century, Wageningen University & Research (WUR) has evolved from agricultural roots into a purpose-driven, interdisciplinary organisation playing a leading role in addressing global challenges in food, nature, and the living environment.
Our mission is grounded in a simple but urgent reality: humanity’s future depends on the health of our planet. We are part of nature and cannot live apart from it.

WUR's duty is clear: find innovative ways to bring production and consumption systems into harmony with nature. We do this through systemic thinking. Connecting disciplines from social to life sciences and linking fundamental research to real-world application. Our unique integration of University and Research enables us to translate knowledge into practice, from lab to land, and from local solutions to global impact.
Together with partners worldwide, we address complex challenges such as food security, climate adaptation, biodiversity, and health, contributing to the Sustainable Development Goals.
Everyone at WUR, students, researchers, teachers and staff, shares an intrinsic and pragmatic drive to shape a sustainable future. Developing knowledge and applying it where it makes a difference. This results in high-quality education, impactful research, and strong international collaboration.
This commitment is reflected in our global standing. WUR consistently ranks among the world’s leading universities in our domain. Rankings are not an end in themselves, but a reflection of the relevance and real-world impact of our science and education, and of our ambition to help create a future in which humanity and nature thrive in balance.
WUR offers a broad range of bachelor’s and master’s programmes:
8 English-taught bachelor’s programmes  
40+ master’s programmes  
over 64,000 alumni

About the University of Amsterdam
Basic information and contact details for the University of Amsterdam
At the University of Amsterdam (UvA) students can choose from over 200 English-taught degree programmes – including some that are unique to this university. The UvA ranks 58th in Times Higher World Rankings 2025 and is the 2nd Dutch university in the THE Europe Teaching Rankings. With over 14,000 international students and researchers from more than 100 countries, the UvA offers one of the widest range of English-taught master’s studies in Europe.

Tracing its roots to the establishment of the Athenaeum Illustre in 1632, the UvA is a modern, research-intensive university located in the heart of a vibrant European capital city. Do you have the intellect and ambition to join our innovative academic community? We welcome applications from open-minded students who want to broaden their international outlook, gain knowledge and skills for their career and help solve complex world issues. Learn more about our Bachelor’s programmes and our Master’s programmes on our website.
About the UvA
Prime location: The UvA’s home city is Amsterdam, a vibrant creative, European cultural and business hub. Amsterdam ranks 6th worldwide in Mercer's 2024 ‘Quality of Living Survey’, 2nd in Europe and 6th globally in The Economist’s Safe Cities Index 2021..
Wide choice of degrees: The University of Amsterdam offers over 200 English-taught degree programmes – one of the largest selections of any university in Europe.
Ranking, research, reputation: The UvA ranks among the top 20 universities in Europe and the top 65 worldwide in various world rankings. Accredited by the Dutch government and the NVAO, it is a member of the League of European Research Universities (LERU) and Universitas 21.
EU and global connections: Over 15,000 of the University’s 43,000 students come from outside the Netherlands, from over 100 countries. As an UvA student, you can expect to gain new perspectives, broaden your international network and strengthen your global mindset.

As with last year, the UvA is in 62nd place in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027. The rankings were published on Wednesday, 30 September.
The UvA is the second-highest ranked Dutch university on the list. A total of five Dutch universities feature in the top 100. In addition to the UvA, these are TU Delft, Wageningen University, Leiden University, and the University of Groningen. TU Delft holds the highest position—as it did last year—and has climbed to 50th place overall.
The global top three remains almost unchanged from last year. The University of Oxford is ranked number one, followed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in second place. Third place is shared this year by Princeton University and Stanford University; last year, it was Cambridge University that shared the third spot with Princeton.

## **Method**
The rankings are based on 18 performance indicators, divided into five areas: Teaching (the learning environment): 29.5%; Research environment (volume, income, and reputation): 29%; Research quality (citation impact, research strength, research excellence, and research influence): 30%; International outlook (staff, students, and research): 7.5%; and Industry (income and patents): 4%. The UvA scores highest in the Research quality category.

## Cookie Consent
De UvA gebruikt cookies voor het meten, optimaliseren en goed laten functioneren van de website. Ook worden er cookies geplaatst om inhoud van derden te kunnen tonen en voor marketingdoeleinden. Klik op ‘Accepteren’ om akkoord te gaan met het plaatsen van alle cookies. Of kies voor ‘Weigeren’ om alleen functionele en analytische cookies te accepteren. Je kunt je voorkeur op ieder moment wijzigen door op de link ‘Cookie instellingen’ te klikken die je onderaan iedere pagina vindt. Lees ook het UvA Privacy statement.

As with last year, the UvA is in 62nd place in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027. The rankings were published on Wednesday, 30 September.
The UvA is the second-highest ranked Dutch university on the list. A total of five Dutch universities feature in the top 100. In addition to the UvA, these are TU Delft, Wageningen University, Leiden University, and the University of Groningen. TU Delft holds the highest position—as it did last year—and has climbed to 50th place overall.
The global top three remains almost unchanged from last year. The University of Oxford is ranked number one, followed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in second place. Third place is shared this year by Princeton University and Stanford University; last year, it was Cambridge University that shared the third spot with Princeton.
texts.1:
## **Method**
The rankings are based on 18 performance indicators, divided into five areas: Teaching (the learning environment): 29.5%; Research environment (volume, income, and reputation): 29%; Research quality (citation impact, research strength, research excellence, and research influence): 30%; International outlook (staff, students, and research): 7.5%; and Industry (income and patents): 4%. The UvA scores highest in the Research quality category.

Title: Nutri-Score
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
## What is Nutri-Score?
Nutri-Score is a food choice logo from France and helps to choose products with a better composition. The logo gives an overall score for a food product based on the nutritional value, looking at the positives and negatives of the product. Examples of negatives are calories, sugar, saturated fat and salt. Positives are vegetables, fruit, legumes, fibre and protein.
The system gives points for each positive or negative based on the ceiling limit for its amount in the product. Next, it deducts the points for the positives from the points for the negatives to give a total score. Based on this total score, it gives the product an A, B, C, D or E. A dark green ‘A’ means the product has a better composition than the same type of product with a dark orange ‘E’. It does not mean that a product with an A or B is healthy, but it is a better choice than the same type of product with an orange D.
Food choice logos like Nutri-Score help people compare products and make better food choices. De Nutri-Score is especially useful for foods that are not included in the Wheel of Five. The Wheel of Five remains the advice for healthy food. For more information about Nutri-Score, see Nutriscore.nl (link is external). A calculation tool (link is external)is available for companies. They can use it to calculate a product’s Nutri-Score.

## What is RIVM’s role in Nutri-Score?
The Netherlands and six other countries are working out how to use the Nutri-Score food choice logo and make its use easier. The other countries are France, Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain and Switzerland. They are working together in two international bodies: a steering group and a scientific committee. RIVM and the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport are both representing the Netherlands in these bodies.
The steering group is coordinating the introduction of Nutri-Score in each country. Nutri-Score uses an algorithm to calculate a food product’s score. The scientific committee is investigating if changes to this algorithm can help match the score to the countries’ dietary guidelines. And if so, how. RIVM is working on a literature review and making calculations, so it can offer advice. RIVM is also taking part in working groups and answers the involved parties’ questions about the subject matter and technical aspects on behalf of the international technical committee.

## Study: how to match Nutri-Score to the Wheel of Five
In the run-up to the introduction of a new food choice logo, RIVM worked with the Netherlands Nutrition Centre in 2019 on a study in which three European food choice logos were compared with the Dutch guidelines the Wheel of Five. The three logos were the Scandinavian Keyhole, the British Multiple Traffic Light and the French Nutri-Score. All of these logos were able to help people rank food products based on how healthy they are. Nutri-Score was found to do this slightly better than Multiple Traffic Light. Based on the results of this study, the State Secretary for Health, Welfare and Sport has decided that Nutri-Score is the food choice logo we should use in the Netherlands.
In 2021, RIVM did a study to ascertain the match between Nutri-Score and the Dutch dietary guidelines (link is external). This study revealed that Nutri-Score is not yet a good match for all the food product groups in the Dutch guidelines (for example, cake and pastries, bread and cereal products, milk and dairy beverages, cheese and processed meats). Given this fact, RIVM advised that the Nutri-Score algorithm needed to be updated.

## The updated Nutri-Score algorithm
Because Nutri-Score was originally developed for France, it was not a sufficient match with the dietary guidelines applicable in various European countries. Therefore, the scientific committee launched a study (link is external)to identify how to improve the algorithm’s match with the various dietary guidelines. The algorithm for solid foods (link is external)was updated in 2022, followed by the algorithm for beverages (link is external)in March 2023. The steering group adopted the new algorithms and the Health Council of the Netherlands published an advisory report (link is external) about them. The Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport then decided (link is external)to introduce Nutri-Score in the Netherlands on 1 January 2024 based on the study by the scientific committee and the advisory report of the Health Council of the Netherlands.

## Nutri-Score as a motivator for product improvement?
Food choice logos like Nutri-Score can also motivate companies to improve their products. RIVM investigated this in a theoretical way in2021 (link is external). Lowering the amounts of sugar and salt or raising the amounts of positive ingredients (like the percentage of vegetables in a meal) will improve the Nutri-Score of a product. The company can then sell the product (for example a meal with more vegetables and less salt) as a better choice compared to products that have not been improved. A better Nutri-Score can motivate consumers to choose a particular product.
Recently, RIVM looked at the supply of food products in the Netherlands (link is external)and in various other European countries (link is external). In the Netherlands, breakfast cereals, meat preserves and sweets ands sweets goods had a lower sugar and/or saturated fat content in 2020 compared to 2018. In five European countries, breakfast cereals and processed potato products had less salt and bread products had less sugar between 2019 and 2021. In both studies, the RIVM calculated a more favorable Nutri-Score for these product groups. Nutri-Score could therefore be an incentive for product improvement. Monitoring should show to what extent manufacturers are encouraged by Nutri-Score to improve foods.

## NAPV product criteria and Nutri-Score
In early 2022, RIVM published ceiling limits as part of the National Approach to Product Improvement (NAPV). The limits help producers to lower the amounts of salt, saturated fat and sugar in food products, one step at a time. In July 2023, the ceiling limits were, where possible, brought in line with the (new) Nutri-Score cut-off points.

## Monitoring Nutri-Score
RIVM will monitor the use of Nutri-Score. The distribution of scores A-E and changes in the composition of food products will be monitored as well. Data from the [Food Database (link is external)](https://www.voedingscentrum.nl/professionals/productaanbod-en-levensmiddelendatabank/levensmiddelendatabank.aspx#:~:text=De%20Levensmiddelendatabank%20bevat%20uitgebreide%20etiketinformatie,Volksgezondheid%20en%20Milieu%20(RIVM).) (Levensmiddelendatabank) will be used for this purpose.

## More information (in Dutch and English)

The effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and how this is affected by product prices .
Hester M. Mulder
SNR 2077391
Master Thesis 2023 -2024
Communication and Information Sciences
New Media Design
Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital Science
Tilburg University
Supervisors: Dr. Tessa van Leeuwen
Second reader: Dr. Nienke van der L aan
April 25, 202 4
Study was app roved by the Research Ethics and Data Management Committee of the Tilburg
School of Humanities and Digi tal Science , Tilburg University 2
Abstract
This study investigated the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score in increasing people s’ healthy
food choices in supermarkets , and how the Nutri -Score’s effectiveness is affected by the
product s’ prices. An online survey was conducted in which the participants were asked to do
fic tional grocery shopping. The survey consisted of 16 different products , of which p articipants
were asked to choose between the original product and a healthier variant of that product .
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions which determined whether the
Nutri -Score was displayed or not and whether there was a price difference between the product
variants or not. In case of a price difference, the healthy product was always more expensive than
the original product , and actual supermarket prices were used in our study . The results show that
the display of the Nutri -Score increased the participants’ healthy food choices . However, the
results also show that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score was significantly reduced by a price
difference between the original and healthy variant . With these results we can argue that the
Nutri -Score as a nudge to increase peoples’ healthy food choices was effective in this study .
Nevertheless, the results also demonstrate that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score is not robust
against the price differences between the original product and the healthy variants. This implies
that the use of the Nutri -Score is not enough to increase peoples’ healthy food choices in the
Dutch supermarket s where price differences play a role in the human decision making.
Keywords: Nudges, Front -of -Package Label, Nutri -Score, Decision Making, Product
Prices 3
The effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and how this is affected by product prices

Unhealthy eating behavior and obesity are becoming a maj or challenge for health -care
systems worldwide. Worrying numbers published by The World Health Organization showed
that 1.9 billion adults of 18 years and older were overweight in 2016 and of them, 650 million
were obese (WHO, 2021). Obesity and overweight are partly caused by an increased intake of
energy -dens e and high -processed foods that are high in sugars and fat and form major risk
factors for heart diseases, diabetes, and some cancers (Wright & Aronne, 2012; WHO, 2021).
Therefore, it is critical to i ncrease knowledge about healthy eating and support people in making
healthier food choices.
Various methods to increase people ’s healthiness have demonstrated to have positive
effects, such as apps that allow food tracking, goal setting, activity tracking and feedback
moments (Carter et al., 2013) . It also has been shown that nudges work effectively to encourage
consumers to make healthier food choices (Cadario & Chandon, 2019; Jesse et al., 2021). Thaler
and Sunstein (200 9) defined the term ‘nudges’ as “any aspect of the choice architecture that
alters people’s behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly
changing their economic incentives.” Numerous nudges are found to be successful in
encouraging people to make healthier dietary choices. Kroese et al. (2015) found that
repositioning healthy products, by placing them at the cash register desk, increased the
consumption of these healthy products. A hybrid nudge of social information combined with
setting was also found to be effective in increasing the likelihood that the nudged item was
purchased (Jesse et al., 2021). Another effective nudge for healthy food choices are Front -of -
Package labels (F OP labels ) that give consumers information about the nutrition quality of the
products in supermarkets. 4
The WHO recently recommended the use of F OP labels in order to encourage consumers
to make healthier food choices (WHO, 2021). A study found promising effects of FOP labels on
people’s healthy food choices but also highlights challenges in consumer understanding of these

labels ( Campos et al., 2011). The Nutri -Score is a specific kind of FOP labels and aims for all
consumers to understand the nutritional quality of a food product in a glance . It also aims to
simplify nutrition advice , given by health professionals , in order to increase people’s healthier
food choices (Ministère de la Santé et de la Prévention , 2021).
The Nutri -Score is a five -color scale associated with letters to convey the nutrition al
quality of the product. The scale goes from an “A” in dark green for foods with a higher
nutritional quality to an “E” in dark orange for foods with a lower nutritional quality (Figure 1).
Various scientific studies pointed out the preference for the Nutri -Score compared to other FOP
labels in terms of ease of identification, speed of interpretation, and perception (De Temmerman
et al., 2021; Ducrot e t al., 2015; Julia et al., 2017). This suggests that consumers have a better
understanding of the nutritional quality with the Nutri -Score compared to other FoPLs (Hercberg
et al., 2022).
Nevertheless, in addition to its visual appeal, the Nutri -Score must be successful in
influencing people's healthy food choices. A study conducted by Egnell et al. (2018) tested the
effectiveness of five different FOP labels across 12 different countries and found that the Nutri -
Score performed best in increasing healthier food choices in all countries. Other studies also
found positive effects of the Nutri -Score on people’s healthy food choices in supermarkets (De
Temmerman et al., 2021; Julia & Hercberg, 2017). 5
Figure 1
The design of the Nutri -Score (Julia & Hercberg, 2017)
Despite the promising findings of effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and other nudges,
there is another important factor in the decision -making of people’s food choices that should be
considered: the price of products (Chang, 2009 ; Steenhuis et al., 2011 ; Żakowska‐Biemans,

2011) . Price discounts for healthy food products in combination with nudges showed a positive
effect on the healthy food purchases (Hoenink et al., 2020). However, only a few studies ha ve
yet been conducted how the effectiveness of nudges toward healthier food choices is affected by
healthy food that is more expensive than unhealthy food. Consumers are willing to pay more for
a product with a FOP labels , but only up to an additional price of 3.7% (Cooper et al, 2020).
Research pointed out that consumers tend to believe that healthy food is more expensive
than less healthy food (Haws et al., 2017 ; Jo & Lusk, 2018) . Rao et al. (2013) found that
generally, unhealthy food also cost less than healthier food products. Product prices in the Dutch
supermarket Albert Heijn also show, that sometimes, healthier alternatives of products cost more
than the original variants (Albert Heijn , n.d. ). Since price is an important factor in the
consumer’s decision making, higher prices for healthy food may affect the effectiveness of
nudges, such as the Nutri -Score. Nudges are an important instrument in fighting the worldwide
health crisis by influencing people to make healthier food choices. If prices of healthy products
hold consumers back from choosing these products, it could be a quest for retailers and
manufactu rers to contribute to solving the health crisis by re -evaluating the prices. To investigat e6
how prices of products affect the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score, the following research
question is asked:
What are the effects of the Nutri -Score on consumer s’ healthy food choices and how does the
price of products factor in these choices?
Theoretical Framework
Nudges
The nudging theory derives from the field of behavioral sciences and provides us with a
new opportunity to influence people s’ choices (Thaler & Sunstein, 2009). The decision -making
process is a complex process of which many dual -processing theories have been proposed which
are all very similar (Sanfey & Chang, 2008 ; Schneider & Chein , 2010 ; Brocas & Carrillo, 2014 ).
According to these dual -processing theories, decision -making is frequently ascribed to the

interaction between two different systems of reasoni ng (Diederich & Trueblood, 2018) . Decision
making in s ystem 1 is described as fast, effortless, automatic, emotional and unconscious.
Decision making in s ystem 2 is described as controlled, slow, conscious, rule based and
affectively neutral. Supermarket environmental nudges employ heuristics or environmental cues,
to subtly influence consumers' food decisions, which is an example of system 1 decision -making
(Ha rbers et al ., 2020) . Educational nudges at the individual level, such as FOP labels, engage the
deliberate and laborious processes of system 2 decision making. Therefore, n udges in a
supermarket can affect behavior by changing the context of products which triggers automatic
decisions (Bruns et al., 2018) or by pro vi ding nutritional informa tion which triggers reflective
processes (Marteau et al., 2012) . There are various d ifferent frameworks for types of nudge, and
one of those is the nudging and choice architecture of Wilson et al., (2016) which consists of six 7
different types and is based on Blumenthal -Barby & Burroughs (2012). In Table 1, the six nudge
types are named and described.
Table 1
Nudging and choice architecture categories (Wilson et al., 2016; Blumenthal -Barby &
Burroughs , 2012).
Category Explanation
Priming nudges People are influenced by subconscious cues that can be strategically used
as primes.
Salience nudges People are influenced by personally relevant, novel, or vivid explanations
and examples.
Default nudges People are influenced by preset options.
Incentive nudges People are influenced by reinforcements for a positive choice or
punishments for a negative choice.
Commitments
and Ego nudges
People are influenced by making a commitment or by their need to feel
good about themselves.
Norms and
messenger nudges
People are influenced by comparing themselves to others.
Nudging towards health
The approach of nudging proposes that it is legitimate to influence people’s behavior to
make life safer, simpler, or easier for people without excluding their options and giving them the

freedom of choice (Marteau et al., 2012; Marteau et al. 2011; Sunstein, 2014; Bonell et al.,
2011). Individuals tend to not always take the most beneficial decisions about their health and
welfare, and nudges are therefore a popular type of intervention to increase people’s health 8
(Ledderer et al., 2020). Nudging towards health typically involves arranging the choice
environment in a way that makes the healthy behavior more likely, which is an example of
priming nudges (Blumenthal -Barby & Burroughs , 2012). Subconscious cues are implemented in
the choice environment which guide people to a certain choice. An example of these cues is
applying footprints on stairs to increase employees’ stair use in an office which is an intervention
nudge (Van der Meiden et al., 2019). The digital choi ce environment , on the other hand, is the
user interface (Weinman et al., 2016) . Therefore, for digital nudging, it is the user interface
design that is arranged in certain ways to affect the consumers ’ choices (Mirsch et al., 2017 ).
Most nudges for healthier lifestyle choices are focused on healthier food choices , such as
changing the placement of healthy products in supermarket s, or food tracking apps. Studies
showed positive effects on healthier food choices with the use of priming and salience nudges
such as images and borders that highlight healthier products (Starke et al., 2021; Blom et al .,
2021). Whereas priming nudges are used for unconscious cues in environments and interfaces, a
form of salience nudges are nutrition labels o n the packages of products to influence consumers
by providing nutritional information (Lindstrom, 2021) . This study will focus on the nu trition
labels because of the official introduction of the Nutri -Score in The Netherlands this year which
makes it more relevant to investigate the effectiveness of this nudge.
Salience nudge: Nutrition labels
These so -called ‘Front -of -Package labels’ (FOP labels) are commonly used for products
in supermarkets and indicate the healthiness of the product. FOP labels are created to simplify

nutritional information of products for consumers to help them with makin g healthier food
choices (Van der Bend & Lissner, 2019). In Figure 2, five existing F OP labels are displayed: a)
Health Star Rating system, b) Multiple Traffic Lights, c) Nutri -Score, d) Reference Intakes, and 9
e) Warning Symbol. The health Star Rating system and the Nutri -Score sho w the product’ s
nutritional quality to the consumer with the use of a scale . The Multiple Traffic light and the
Re fe rence Intakes show the amount of nutritional ingredients and what percentage that is of the
re ferred daily intakes. The Warning Symbol warns the consumers for food that have a high
amoun t of a certain nutritional ingredient. All these FOP labels are focused on communicat ing
the nutritional qualit y of a product or warnings about ingredients of the pro duct. FOP l abels can
be online nudge s, disp layed with the corresponding product in an online environment , or offline
nudges on the pac kages of the prod ucts. In this study, the FOP label is applied in an online
environment , which makes it a fo rm of digital nud ging.
Figure 2
Five different types of Front -of -Package labels: a) Health Star Rating System, b) Multiple Traffic
Lights, c) Nutri -Score, d) Reference Intakes, and e) Warning Symbol.
a) b) c)

A meta -analysis that examined 114 articles about the impact of FOP labels showed that

The effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and how this is affected by product prices .
Hester M. Mulder
SNR 2077391
Master Thesis 2023 -2024
Communication and Information Sciences
New Media Design
Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital Science
Tilburg University
Supervisors: Dr. Tessa van Leeuwen
Second reader: Dr. Nienke van der L aan
April 25, 202 4
Study was app roved by the Research Ethics and Data Management Committee of the Tilburg
School of Humanities and Digi tal Science , Tilburg University 2
Abstract
This study investigated the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score in increasing people s’ healthy
food choices in supermarkets , and how the Nutri -Score’s effectiveness is affected by the
product s’ prices. An online survey was conducted in which the participants were asked to do
fic tional grocery shopping. The survey consisted of 16 different products , of which p articipants
were asked to choose between the original product and a healthier variant of that product .
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions which determined whether the
Nutri -Score was displayed or not and whether there was a price difference between the product
variants or not. In case of a price difference, the healthy product was always more expensive than
the original product , and actual supermarket prices were used in our study . The results show that
the display of the Nutri -Score increased the participants’ healthy food choices . However, the
results also show that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score was significantly reduced by a price
difference between the original and healthy variant . With these results we can argue that the
Nutri -Score as a nudge to increase peoples’ healthy food choices was effective in this study .
Nevertheless, the results also demonstrate that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score is not robust
against the price differences between the original product and the healthy variants. This implies
that the use of the Nutri -Score is not enough to increase peoples’ healthy food choices in the
Dutch supermarket s where price differences play a role in the human decision making.
Keywords: Nudges, Front -of -Package Label, Nutri -Score, Decision Making, Product
Prices 3
The effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and how this is affected by product prices
texts.1:
Unhealthy eating behavior and obesity are becoming a maj or challenge for health -care
systems worldwide. Worrying numbers published by The World Health Organization showed
that 1.9 billion adults of 18 years and older were overweight in 2016 and of them, 650 million
were obese (WHO, 2021). Obesity and overweight are partly caused by an increased intake of
energy -dens e and high -processed foods that are high in sugars and fat and form major risk
factors for heart diseases, diabetes, and some cancers (Wright & Aronne, 2012; WHO, 2021).
Therefore, it is critical to i ncrease knowledge about healthy eating and support people in making
healthier food choices.
Various methods to increase people ’s healthiness have demonstrated to have positive
effects, such as apps that allow food tracking, goal setting, activity tracking and feedback
moments (Carter et al., 2013) . It also has been shown that nudges work effectively to encourage
consumers to make healthier food choices (Cadario & Chandon, 2019; Jesse et al., 2021). Thaler
and Sunstein (200 9) defined the term ‘nudges’ as “any aspect of the choice architecture that
alters people’s behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly
changing their economic incentives.” Numerous nudges are found to be successful in
encouraging people to make healthier dietary choices. Kroese et al. (2015) found that
repositioning healthy products, by placing them at the cash register desk, increased the
consumption of these healthy products. A hybrid nudge of social information combined with
setting was also found to be effective in increasing the likelihood that the nudged item was
purchased (Jesse et al., 2021). Another effective nudge for healthy food choices are Front -of -
Package labels (F OP labels ) that give consumers information about the nutrition quality of the
products in supermarkets. 4
The WHO recently recommended the use of F OP labels in order to encourage consumers
to make healthier food choices (WHO, 2021). A study found promising effects of FOP labels on
people’s healthy food choices but also highlights challenges in consumer understanding of these
texts.2:
labels ( Campos et al., 2011). The Nutri -Score is a specific kind of FOP labels and aims for all
consumers to understand the nutritional quality of a food product in a glance . It also aims to
simplify nutrition advice , given by health professionals , in order to increase people’s healthier
food choices (Ministère de la Santé et de la Prévention , 2021).
The Nutri -Score is a five -color scale associated with letters to convey the nutrition al
quality of the product. The scale goes from an “A” in dark green for foods with a higher
nutritional quality to an “E” in dark orange for foods with a lower nutritional quality (Figure 1).
Various scientific studies pointed out the preference for the Nutri -Score compared to other FOP
labels in terms of ease of identification, speed of interpretation, and perception (De Temmerman
et al., 2021; Ducrot e t al., 2015; Julia et al., 2017). This suggests that consumers have a better
understanding of the nutritional quality with the Nutri -Score compared to other FoPLs (Hercberg
et al., 2022).
Nevertheless, in addition to its visual appeal, the Nutri -Score must be successful in
influencing people's healthy food choices. A study conducted by Egnell et al. (2018) tested the
effectiveness of five different FOP labels across 12 different countries and found that the Nutri -
Score performed best in increasing healthier food choices in all countries. Other studies also
found positive effects of the Nutri -Score on people’s healthy food choices in supermarkets (De
Temmerman et al., 2021; Julia & Hercberg, 2017). 5
Figure 1
The design of the Nutri -Score (Julia & Hercberg, 2017)
Despite the promising findings of effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and other nudges,
there is another important factor in the decision -making of people’s food choices that should be
considered: the price of products (Chang, 2009 ; Steenhuis et al., 2011 ; Żakowska‐Biemans,
texts.3:
2011) . Price discounts for healthy food products in combination with nudges showed a positive
effect on the healthy food purchases (Hoenink et al., 2020). However, only a few studies ha ve
yet been conducted how the effectiveness of nudges toward healthier food choices is affected by
healthy food that is more expensive than unhealthy food. Consumers are willing to pay more for
a product with a FOP labels , but only up to an additional price of 3.7% (Cooper et al, 2020).
Research pointed out that consumers tend to believe that healthy food is more expensive
than less healthy food (Haws et al., 2017 ; Jo & Lusk, 2018) . Rao et al. (2013) found that
generally, unhealthy food also cost less than healthier food products. Product prices in the Dutch
supermarket Albert Heijn also show, that sometimes, healthier alternatives of products cost more
than the original variants (Albert Heijn , n.d. ). Since price is an important factor in the
consumer’s decision making, higher prices for healthy food may affect the effectiveness of
nudges, such as the Nutri -Score. Nudges are an important instrument in fighting the worldwide
health crisis by influencing people to make healthier food choices. If prices of healthy products
hold consumers back from choosing these products, it could be a quest for retailers and
manufactu rers to contribute to solving the health crisis by re -evaluating the prices. To investigat e6
how prices of products affect the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score, the following research
question is asked:
What are the effects of the Nutri -Score on consumer s’ healthy food choices and how does the
price of products factor in these choices?
Theoretical Framework
Nudges
The nudging theory derives from the field of behavioral sciences and provides us with a
new opportunity to influence people s’ choices (Thaler & Sunstein, 2009). The decision -making
process is a complex process of which many dual -processing theories have been proposed which
are all very similar (Sanfey & Chang, 2008 ; Schneider & Chein , 2010 ; Brocas & Carrillo, 2014 ).
According to these dual -processing theories, decision -making is frequently ascribed to the
texts.4:
interaction between two different systems of reasoni ng (Diederich & Trueblood, 2018) . Decision
making in s ystem 1 is described as fast, effortless, automatic, emotional and unconscious.
Decision making in s ystem 2 is described as controlled, slow, conscious, rule based and
affectively neutral. Supermarket environmental nudges employ heuristics or environmental cues,
to subtly influence consumers' food decisions, which is an example of system 1 decision -making
(Ha rbers et al ., 2020) . Educational nudges at the individual level, such as FOP labels, engage the
deliberate and laborious processes of system 2 decision making. Therefore, n udges in a
supermarket can affect behavior by changing the context of products which triggers automatic
decisions (Bruns et al., 2018) or by pro vi ding nutritional informa tion which triggers reflective
processes (Marteau et al., 2012) . There are various d ifferent frameworks for types of nudge, and
one of those is the nudging and choice architecture of Wilson et al., (2016) which consists of six 7
different types and is based on Blumenthal -Barby & Burroughs (2012). In Table 1, the six nudge
types are named and described.
Table 1
Nudging and choice architecture categories (Wilson et al., 2016; Blumenthal -Barby &
Burroughs , 2012).
Category Explanation
Priming nudges People are influenced by subconscious cues that can be strategically used
as primes.
Salience nudges People are influenced by personally relevant, novel, or vivid explanations
and examples.
Default nudges People are influenced by preset options.
Incentive nudges People are influenced by reinforcements for a positive choice or
punishments for a negative choice.
Commitments
and Ego nudges
People are influenced by making a commitment or by their need to feel
good about themselves.
Norms and
messenger nudges
People are influenced by comparing themselves to others.
Nudging towards health
The approach of nudging proposes that it is legitimate to influence people’s behavior to
make life safer, simpler, or easier for people without excluding their options and giving them the
texts.5:
freedom of choice (Marteau et al., 2012; Marteau et al. 2011; Sunstein, 2014; Bonell et al.,
2011). Individuals tend to not always take the most beneficial decisions about their health and
welfare, and nudges are therefore a popular type of intervention to increase people’s health 8
(Ledderer et al., 2020). Nudging towards health typically involves arranging the choice
environment in a way that makes the healthy behavior more likely, which is an example of
priming nudges (Blumenthal -Barby & Burroughs , 2012). Subconscious cues are implemented in
the choice environment which guide people to a certain choice. An example of these cues is
applying footprints on stairs to increase employees’ stair use in an office which is an intervention
nudge (Van der Meiden et al., 2019). The digital choi ce environment , on the other hand, is the
user interface (Weinman et al., 2016) . Therefore, for digital nudging, it is the user interface
design that is arranged in certain ways to affect the consumers ’ choices (Mirsch et al., 2017 ).
Most nudges for healthier lifestyle choices are focused on healthier food choices , such as
changing the placement of healthy products in supermarket s, or food tracking apps. Studies
showed positive effects on healthier food choices with the use of priming and salience nudges
such as images and borders that highlight healthier products (Starke et al., 2021; Blom et al .,
2021). Whereas priming nudges are used for unconscious cues in environments and interfaces, a
form of salience nudges are nutrition labels o n the packages of products to influence consumers
by providing nutritional information (Lindstrom, 2021) . This study will focus on the nu trition
labels because of the official introduction of the Nutri -Score in The Netherlands this year which
makes it more relevant to investigate the effectiveness of this nudge.
Salience nudge: Nutrition labels
These so -called ‘Front -of -Package labels’ (FOP labels) are commonly used for products
in supermarkets and indicate the healthiness of the product. FOP labels are created to simplify
texts.6:
nutritional information of products for consumers to help them with makin g healthier food
choices (Van der Bend & Lissner, 2019). In Figure 2, five existing F OP labels are displayed: a)
Health Star Rating system, b) Multiple Traffic Lights, c) Nutri -Score, d) Reference Intakes, and 9
e) Warning Symbol. The health Star Rating system and the Nutri -Score sho w the product’ s
nutritional quality to the consumer with the use of a scale . The Multiple Traffic light and the
Re fe rence Intakes show the amount of nutritional ingredients and what percentage that is of the
re ferred daily intakes. The Warning Symbol warns the consumers for food that have a high
amoun t of a certain nutritional ingredient. All these FOP labels are focused on communicat ing
the nutritional qualit y of a product or warnings about ingredients of the pro duct. FOP l abels can
be online nudge s, disp layed with the corresponding product in an online environment , or offline
nudges on the pac kages of the prod ucts. In this study, the FOP label is applied in an online
environment , which makes it a fo rm of digital nud ging.

Lights, c) Nutri -Score, d) Reference Intakes, and e) Warning Symbol.

## What is Nutri-Score?
Nutri-Score is a food choice logo from France and helps to choose products with a better composition. The logo gives an overall score for a food product based on the nutritional value, looking at the positives and negatives of the product. Examples of negatives are calories, sugar, saturated fat and salt. Positives are vegetables, fruit, legumes, fibre and protein.
The system gives points for each positive or negative based on the ceiling limit for its amount in the product. Next, it deducts the points for the positives from the points for the negatives to give a total score. Based on this total score, it gives the product an A, B, C, D or E. A dark green ‘A’ means the product has a better composition than the same type of product with a dark orange ‘E’. It does not mean that a product with an A or B is healthy, but it is a better choice than the same type of product with an orange D.
Food choice logos like Nutri-Score help people compare products and make better food choices. De Nutri-Score is especially useful for foods that are not included in the Wheel of Five. The Wheel of Five remains the advice for healthy food. For more information about Nutri-Score, see Nutriscore.nl (link is external). A calculation tool (link is external)is available for companies. They can use it to calculate a product’s Nutri-Score.
texts.1:
## What is RIVM’s role in Nutri-Score?
The Netherlands and six other countries are working out how to use the Nutri-Score food choice logo and make its use easier. The other countries are France, Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain and Switzerland. They are working together in two international bodies: a steering group and a scientific committee. RIVM and the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport are both representing the Netherlands in these bodies.
The steering group is coordinating the introduction of Nutri-Score in each country. Nutri-Score uses an algorithm to calculate a food product’s score. The scientific committee is investigating if changes to this algorithm can help match the score to the countries’ dietary guidelines. And if so, how. RIVM is working on a literature review and making calculations, so it can offer advice. RIVM is also taking part in working groups and answers the involved parties’ questions about the subject matter and technical aspects on behalf of the international technical committee.
texts.2:
## Study: how to match Nutri-Score to the Wheel of Five
In the run-up to the introduction of a new food choice logo, RIVM worked with the Netherlands Nutrition Centre in 2019 on a study in which three European food choice logos were compared with the Dutch guidelines the Wheel of Five. The three logos were the Scandinavian Keyhole, the British Multiple Traffic Light and the French Nutri-Score. All of these logos were able to help people rank food products based on how healthy they are. Nutri-Score was found to do this slightly better than Multiple Traffic Light. Based on the results of this study, the State Secretary for Health, Welfare and Sport has decided that Nutri-Score is the food choice logo we should use in the Netherlands.
In 2021, RIVM did a study to ascertain the match between Nutri-Score and the Dutch dietary guidelines (link is external). This study revealed that Nutri-Score is not yet a good match for all the food product groups in the Dutch guidelines (for example, cake and pastries, bread and cereal products, milk and dairy beverages, cheese and processed meats). Given this fact, RIVM advised that the Nutri-Score algorithm needed to be updated.
texts.3:
## The updated Nutri-Score algorithm
Because Nutri-Score was originally developed for France, it was not a sufficient match with the dietary guidelines applicable in various European countries. Therefore, the scientific committee launched a study (link is external)to identify how to improve the algorithm’s match with the various dietary guidelines. The algorithm for solid foods (link is external)was updated in 2022, followed by the algorithm for beverages (link is external)in March 2023. The steering group adopted the new algorithms and the Health Council of the Netherlands published an advisory report (link is external) about them. The Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport then decided (link is external)to introduce Nutri-Score in the Netherlands on 1 January 2024 based on the study by the scientific committee and the advisory report of the Health Council of the Netherlands.
texts.4:
## Nutri-Score as a motivator for product improvement?
Food choice logos like Nutri-Score can also motivate companies to improve their products. RIVM investigated this in a theoretical way in2021 (link is external). Lowering the amounts of sugar and salt or raising the amounts of positive ingredients (like the percentage of vegetables in a meal) will improve the Nutri-Score of a product. The company can then sell the product (for example a meal with more vegetables and less salt) as a better choice compared to products that have not been improved. A better Nutri-Score can motivate consumers to choose a particular product.
Recently, RIVM looked at the supply of food products in the Netherlands (link is external)and in various other European countries (link is external). In the Netherlands, breakfast cereals, meat preserves and sweets ands sweets goods had a lower sugar and/or saturated fat content in 2020 compared to 2018. In five European countries, breakfast cereals and processed potato products had less salt and bread products had less sugar between 2019 and 2021. In both studies, the RIVM calculated a more favorable Nutri-Score for these product groups. Nutri-Score could therefore be an incentive for product improvement. Monitoring should show to what extent manufacturers are encouraged by Nutri-Score to improve foods.
texts.5:
## NAPV product criteria and Nutri-Score
In early 2022, RIVM published ceiling limits as part of the National Approach to Product Improvement (NAPV). The limits help producers to lower the amounts of salt, saturated fat and sugar in food products, one step at a time. In July 2023, the ceiling limits were, where possible, brought in line with the (new) Nutri-Score cut-off points.
texts.6:
## Monitoring Nutri-Score
RIVM will monitor the use of Nutri-Score. The distribution of scores A-E and changes in the composition of food products will be monitored as well. Data from the [Food Database (link is external)](https://www.voedingscentrum.nl/professionals/productaanbod-en-levensmiddelendatabank/levensmiddelendatabank.aspx#:~:text=De%20Levensmiddelendatabank%20bevat%20uitgebreide%20etiketinformatie,Volksgezondheid%20en%20Milieu%20(RIVM).) (Levensmiddelendatabank) will be used for this purpose.

Abstract
This study investigated the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score in increasing people s’ healthy
food choices in supermarkets , and how the Nutri -Score’s effectiveness is affected by the
product s’ prices. An online survey was conducted in which the participants were asked to do
fic tional grocery shopping. The survey consisted of 16 different products , of which p articipants
were asked to choose between the original product and a healthier variant of that product .
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions which determined whether the
Nutri -Score was displayed or not and whether there was a price difference between the product
variants or not. In case of a price difference, the healthy product was always more expensive than
the original product , and actual supermarket prices were used in our study . The results show that
the display of the Nutri -Score increased the participants’ healthy food choices . However, the
results also show that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score was significantly reduced by a price
difference between the original and healthy variant . With these results we can argue that the
Nutri -Score as a nudge to increase peoples’ healthy food choices was effective in this study .
Nevertheless, the results also demonstrate that the effectiveness of the Nutri -Score is not robust
against the price differences between the original product and the healthy variants. This implies
that the use of the Nutri -Score is not enough to increase peoples’ healthy food choices in the
Dutch supermarket s where price differences play a role in the human decision making.
Keywords: Nudges, Front -of -Package Label, Nutri -Score, Decision Making, Product

The effectiveness of the Nutri -Score and how this is affected by product prices

Unhealthy eating behavior and obesity are becoming a maj or challenge for health -care
systems worldwide. Worrying numbers published by The World Health Organization showed
that 1.9 billion adults of 18 years and older were overweight in 2016 and of them, 650 million
were obese (WHO, 2021). Obesity and overweight are partly caused by an increased intake of
energy -dens e and high -processed foods that are high in sugars and fat and form major risk
factors for heart diseases, diabetes, and some cancers (Wright & Aronne, 2012; WHO, 2021).
Therefore, it is critical to i ncrease knowledge about healthy eating and support people in making
healthier food choices.
Various methods to increase people ’s healthiness have demonstrated to have positive
effects, such as apps that allow food tracking, goal setting, activity tracking and feedback
moments (Carter et al., 2013) . It also has been shown that nudges work effectively to encourage
consumers to make healthier food choices (Cadario & Chandon, 2019; Jesse et al., 2021). Thaler
and Sunstein (200 9) defined the term ‘nudges’ as “any aspect of the choice architecture that
alters people’s behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly
changing their economic incentives.” Numerous nudges are found to be successful in
encouraging people to make healthier dietary choices. Kroese et al. (2015) found that
repositioning healthy products, by placing them at the cash register desk, increased the
consumption of these healthy products. A hybrid nudge of social information combined with
setting was also found to be effective in increasing the likelihood that the nudged item was
purchased (Jesse et al., 2021). Another effective nudge for healthy food choices are Front -of -
Package labels (F OP labels ) that give consumers information about the nutrition quality of the
products in supermarkets. 4
The WHO recently recommended the use of F OP labels in order to encourage consumers
to make healthier food choices (WHO, 2021). A study found promising effects of FOP labels on
people’s healthy food choices but also highlights challenges in consumer understanding of these

labels ( Campos et al., 2011). The Nutri -Score is a specific kind of FOP labels and aims for all
consumers to understand the nutritional quality of a food product in a glance . It also aims to
simplify nutrition advice , given by health professionals , in order to increase people’s healthier
food choices (Ministère de la Santé et de la Prévention , 2021).
The Nutri -Score is a five -color scale associated with letters to convey the nutrition al
quality of the product. The scale goes from an “A” in dark green for foods with a higher
nutritional quality to an “E” in dark orange for foods with a lower nutritional quality (Figure 1).
Various scientific studies pointed out the preference for the Nutri -Score compared to other FOP
labels in terms of ease of identification, speed of interpretation, and perception (De Temmerman
et al., 2021; Ducrot e t al., 2015; Julia et al., 2017). This suggests that consumers have a better
understanding of the nutritional quality with the Nutri -Score compared to other FoPLs (Hercberg
et al., 2022).
Nevertheless, in addition to its visual appeal, the Nutri -Score must be successful in
influencing people's healthy food choices. A study conducted by Egnell et al. (2018) tested the
effectiveness of five different FOP labels across 12 different countries and found that the Nutri -
Score performed best in increasing healthier food choices in all countries. Other studies also
found positive effects of the Nutri -Score on people’s healthy food choices in supermarkets (De
Temmerman et al., 2021; Julia & Hercberg, 2017). 5
